# The River of Attention

There is a peculiar moment that occurs when you look up from your phone and realize that an hour has passed, though you could not say where it went. The light in the room has shifted. The tea has gone cold. Somewhere outside, a bird was singing the whole time, and you did not hear it. This small loss may seem trivial, the cost of living in a connected world, but it points to something larger: the way we spend our attention is the way we spend our lives. Attention is not merely a cognitive function; it is the raw material of experience. What we notice becomes our world, and what we fail to notice never quite exists for us.

I want to think about attention not as a productivity metric but as a form of love, a kind of presence, and a quiet art that is increasingly endangered. The modern world has engineered distraction into every crevice of daily life. Alerts, feeds, recommendations, autoplay, infinite scroll—these are not neutral tools. They are designed to capture and hold the one resource that cannot be renewed once spent: the stream of conscious awareness. And yet, beneath the noise, there remains a deeper capacity for sustained, tender attention that can be cultivated. This essay is an attempt to trace what attention is, why it matters, and how we might begin to reclaim it.

To begin, consider what attention actually is. William James, the philosopher and psychologist, wrote in 1890 that “my experience is what I agree to attend to.” This is a radical statement. It suggests that we are not passive recipients of a pre-existing world but active participants in its creation. The world is infinitely rich, too full of detail for any mind to take in completely. Attention is the filter that selects, from the blooming, buzzing confusion of sensory input, the small slice that becomes our reality. If you spend your morning attending to your breath, the patterns of sunlight on the wall, the taste of coffee, you will have lived a different morning than if you spent it scrolling through news of disasters and strangers’ opinions. Both mornings occur in the same chronological time, but they are not the same life.

The difficulty is that attention feels automatic, but it is shaped by forces we often do not see. In the past two decades, an entire economy has grown up around the harvesting of human attention. Social media platforms, news sites, and apps are built to exploit the brain’s reward systems, offering variable rewards—likes, comments, new posts—that keep us checking and refreshing. The psychologist B.F. Skinner discovered decades ago that intermittent reinforcement is the most powerful way to condition behavior. Slot machines use this principle; so do our phones. Each pull of the scroll may yield something delightful or nothing at all, and that unpredictability keeps the loop running. The result is a population that finds it increasingly difficult to read a book, to sit in silence, to look at a painting for more than a few seconds, or to listen to a friend without glancing at a screen.

This is not a moral failing. It is the predictable outcome of designing technology to maximize engagement rather than human flourishing. The algorithms are not evil; they are simply optimizing for a different goal. But the cost is real. When attention is fragmented, the quality of experience degrades. We skim instead of read. We glance instead of see. We hear instead of listen. The world becomes a blur of impressions, none of them deep enough to leave a lasting mark. The poet Mary Oliver wrote, “Attention is the beginning of devotion.” If she is right, then a distracted life is not merely less productive; it is less devoted, less loving, less alive.

Perhaps the most powerful counterforce to the attention economy is the natural world. Nature does not demand our attention; it simply rewards it. A forest, a shoreline, a mountain, a garden—these places move at a different pace. They are not optimized for engagement. They do not send notifications. They are endlessly complex, but their complexity is patient. When you sit by a river and watch the water, nothing happens, and yet everything happens. The light changes. The current shifts. A fish rises. A leaf falls. The longer you look, the more you see. This is the opposite of the rapid switching required by digital media. It is attention as immersion, as participation, as relationship.

The naturalist and writer Annie Dillard spent a year living by Tinker Creek in Virginia, and her book *Pilgrim at Tinker Creek* is a record of what happens when you pay close, sustained attention to a small patch of earth. She noticed the way a frog’s skin color changes as it is eaten by a giant water bug, the way a cedar tree bends in the wind, the way the same creek looks different every hour of the day. She wrote, “I cannot cause light; the most I can do is try to put myself in the path of its beam.” Attention is like that. We cannot force moments of insight or beauty, but we can place ourselves where they are more likely to occur. We can sit still. We can look closely. We can wait.

There is a tradition in Japanese aesthetics called *mono no aware*, often translated as “the pathos of things” or “an empathy toward things.” It is the awareness of impermanence and the gentle sadness that comes from recognizing the beauty of a passing moment. To practice mono no aware is to attend to the cherry blossoms not despite their brevity but because of it. It is to notice the way the light falls on a bowl of fruit, the sound of rain on a tin roof, the smell of wet earth after a storm. These experiences are available to everyone, but they are missed by those whose attention is elsewhere. The art of noticing is not about adding more experiences to our lives; it is about deepening the ones we already have.

Attention also lies at the heart of love. To love someone is to pay attention to them—not just to their words but to their silences, their gestures, their moods, their needs. The philosopher Iris Murdoch argued that love is “the extremely difficult realization that something other than oneself is real.” This realization requires attention. When we truly listen to another person, we set aside our own mental chatter and make space for their reality. We notice the slight hesitation in their voice, the way they avoid a certain topic, the flicker of joy or pain that crosses their face. This kind of attention is a gift. It says, “You matter. Your experience is worth my time.”

In an age of constant partial attention, this kind of listening has become rare. We sit across from loved ones at dinner, half-listening while our minds scroll through to-do lists or our hands rest on the phone in our pocket. We have all been on both sides of this dynamic: speaking to someone who is not fully present, and feeling the subtle hurt of being only half-heard. The remedy is not complicated, but it is difficult. It requires putting the phone away, making eye contact, and choosing to be fully where we are. It requires accepting that we cannot be everywhere at once, and that the person in front of us deserves our whole attention, not the scraps left over after the digital world has taken its share.

Attention is also the foundation of creativity. The psychologist Mihaly Csikszentmihalyi studied what he called “flow,” a state of complete absorption in an activity where time seems to disappear and the self feels merged with the work. Flow occurs when attention is fully focused, when the challenge of the task matches our skills, and when we are free from interruptions. Artists, musicians, writers, scientists, and athletes all describe this state as the source of their best work. But flow is fragile. It takes an average of twenty-three minutes to regain deep focus after an interruption, according to some studies. If we check our email every few minutes, if we respond to every notification, we never enter the sustained concentration that creativity requires. The result is a life of shallow tasks, none of them done with the full force of our abilities.

The poet Rainer Maria Rilke wrote in *Letters to a Young Poet* that “being an artist means not numbering and counting, but ripening like a tree, which does not force its sap and stands confidently in the storms of spring, not afraid that afterward summer may not come.” This ripening requires patience and attention. It requires sitting with an idea long enough for it to develop roots. It requires looking at the world not as a series of problems to be solved but as a mystery to be inhabited. The creative act begins with perception. Before you can write a poem, you must notice something worth writing about. Before you can paint a picture, you must see the light in a way others have not. Before you can compose a song, you must hear the rhythm in everyday life. Attention is the soil in which creativity grows.

It is worth remembering that this capacity for deep attention was not always so rare. The historian of reading Alberto Manguel has described how, in the age before print, reading was often done aloud, slowly, in community. Monks practiced *lectio divina*, a slow, meditative reading of sacred texts, chewing over each word, allowing the meaning to sink into the bones. The act of reading was not about consuming information but about transformation. Today, reading has become something else: a race to finish, a collection of titles to display, a skimming for useful facts. But the old way is still available. We can still read slowly, pausing to let a sentence echo, rereading a passage until it opens. We can still treat a book as a companion rather than a task.

Children understand attention instinctively. Watch a small child playing with a stick or a puddle. They are completely absorbed. They are not checking the time. They are not documenting the moment for later. They are simply there, inside the experience. As we grow older, we learn to divide our attention, to multitask, to be productive. We call this maturity, but it is also a loss. The child’s ability to lose herself in play is a form of attention we should envy and try to recover. It is a reminder that attention is not always about effort. Sometimes it is about surrender, about allowing ourselves to be captured by something outside ourselves.

Boredom has a role to play in this recovery. We are so afraid of boredom that we fill every spare moment with stimulation. Waiting in line, we check our phones. Riding the bus, we listen to podcasts. Eating alone, we watch videos. But boredom is not emptiness; it is a threshold. When we allow ourselves to be bored, our minds begin to wander, to make connections, to notice things. The poet W.H. Auden wrote that “the surest sign of a spiritual life is the capacity to be bored.” Boredom is the doorway through which attention must pass to reach its deeper chambers. If we never let ourselves be bored, we never discover what lies on the other side.

There is a story about the philosopher Socrates, who was known for stopping in his tracks and standing still for hours, lost in thought. His friends would wait, knowing that he was attending to something in his mind. This kind of stillness is almost unthinkable today. We are uncomfortable with silence, with the absence of stimulation. And yet silence is precisely where attention can gather itself. The composer John Cage wrote a piece called *4'33"* in which the performer sits at a piano for four minutes and thirty-three seconds without playing a note. The point is not the absence of music but the presence of the ambient sounds that we normally ignore: the rustle of the audience, the hum of the air conditioner, the distant traffic. Attention to silence reveals that silence is full. The same is true of our inner lives. When we stop filling every moment with noise, we begin to hear the quieter voices of our own thoughts, our own desires, our own questions.

How, then, might we begin to reclaim our attention? The practices are simple to name but difficult to sustain. One is to create periods of intentional solitude. Solitude is not loneliness; it is the choice to be alone with one’s own mind. In solitude, we can read a book without checking our phone. We can take a walk without listening to a podcast. We can sit with a cup of tea and watch the light move across the room. These small acts are not escapes from the world; they are returns to it. By stepping back from the noise, we sharpen our capacity to engage with what matters.

Another practice is to cultivate a habit of close observation. This can be as simple as choosing a small object—a leaf, a stone, a piece of fruit—and looking at it for five minutes, noticing its texture, its color, its shape, its shadows. Or it can be as grand as keeping a journal of daily observations, writing down one thing you noticed each day that you would normally have missed. The point is not to produce great insights but to train the mind to dwell. The artist and educator Frederick Franck wrote a book called *The Zen of Seeing*, in which he describes drawing as a form of meditation. When you draw something, you must look at it with an intensity that most of us rarely exercise. Franck wrote, “I have learned that what I have not drawn, I have never really seen.” Attention is like that. It is the difference between glancing and seeing.

A third practice is to practice listening—to other people, to music, to the natural world. Listening is an act of surrender. You cannot listen while preparing your response. You cannot listen while checking your phone. You must be silent. You must be patient. You must be willing to be changed by what you hear. The Quaker tradition speaks of “listening in silence” as a way of discerning truth. The composer Pauline Oliveros developed a practice called “deep listening,” which she defined as “listening in every possible way to everything possible to hear no matter what you are doing.” This kind of listening is not passive. It is active, engaged, curious. It treats sound as a world to be explored.

Finally, we might practice the art of doing one thing at a time. Multitasking is a myth. The brain does not do two cognitive tasks simultaneously; it switches rapidly between them, and each switch imposes a cost. When we eat, we should eat. When we walk, we should walk. When we talk with a friend, we should talk. This sounds simple, but it is radically countercultural. It means refusing the pressure to optimize every moment, to fill every gap with productivity. It means allowing some experiences to be sufficient in themselves, not as means to an end but as ends in themselves. A meal can be just a meal. A conversation can be just a conversation. A walk can be just a walk. In that just-ness, there is a quiet richness.

At the deepest level, attention is bound up with mortality. We have a finite number of days, a finite number of hours, a finite number of breaths. Every moment we spend in distraction is a moment we will never get back. The Stoic philosopher Seneca wrote that “we are not given a short life but we make it short, and we are not ill-supplied but wasteful of it.” This is not meant to induce anxiety but to inspire clarity. Knowing that time is limited can sharpen our attention. It can help us choose what to notice, what to care about, what to love. The poet William Blake wrote of seeing “a world in a grain of sand and a heaven in a wildflower.” That vision is available to all of us, but it requires attention. It requires the willingness to look at a grain of sand as if it were a world.

I think of the last time I truly paid attention to something beautiful. Perhaps it was the way the morning light caught the edge of a glass of water, creating a small rainbow on the table. Perhaps it was the sound of wind through pine needles, a sound like a distant ocean. Perhaps it was the face of someone I love, seen for a moment not as familiar but as astonishing. These moments are not rare because beauty is rare; they are rare because attention is rare. The world is filled with more beauty than we could ever exhaust. The question is whether we will stop long enough to see it.

The attention economy profits from our distraction, but the choice ultimately remains ours. We can decide to turn off the notifications, to leave the phone in another room, to take a walk without a destination, to look at the sky. We can decide to be present to our own lives. This is not a retreat from the world; it is an engagement with it on a deeper level. It is a small act of resistance, a quiet refusal to live on someone else’s terms. It is the beginning of devotion.

In the end, attention is not about productivity or efficiency. It is about the quality of our presence. It is about whether we are truly here, in this moment, with this person, in this place. It is about whether we see the world as a backdrop for our plans or as a living reality that deserves our regard. The philosopher Simone Weil wrote, “Attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity.” To give someone your attention is to give them a part of your life. To give your attention to a tree, a cloud, a piece of music, a problem, a question—this is to honor the world by taking it seriously. It is to say, “I am here. I am listening. I am looking. I am not going anywhere.” That is, perhaps, the deepest freedom we have. And it begins with a single act of notice, now, in this very moment, if we choose to give it.

So let us practice attention. Let us put down the phone and look out the window. Let us close the laptop and go outside. Let us listen to the birds, to the rain, to the silence, to each other. Let us read slowly, think deeply, and love with our whole being. The world is waiting to be seen. And we, with our limited days and our boundless capacity for wonder, are the ones who can see it. The choice is before us every morning: to sleepwalk through life or to wake up. Attention is the waking. It is the light we bring to the world, and the world, in return, gives us itself. That is a fair exchange. That is, perhaps, the only exchange that matters. And it is available to all of us, in every ordinary moment, if only we will attend.

**The River of Attention**

There is a peculiar moment that occurs when you look up from your phone and realize that an hour has passed, though you could not say where it went. The light in the room has shifted. The tea has gone cold. Somewhere outside, a bird was singing the whole time, and you did not hear it. This small loss may seem trivial, the cost of living in a connected world, but it points to something larger: the way we spend our attention is the way we spend our lives. Attention is not merely a cognitive function; it is the raw material of experience. What we notice becomes our world, and what we fail to notice never quite exists for us.

I want to think about attention not as a productivity metric but as a form of love, a kind of presence, and a quiet art that is increasingly endangered. The modern world has engineered distraction into every crevice of daily life. Alerts, feeds, recommendations, autoplay, infinite scroll—these are not neutral tools. They are designed to capture and hold the one resource that cannot be renewed once spent: the stream of conscious awareness. And yet, beneath the noise, there remains a deeper capacity for sustained, tender attention that can be cultivated. This essay is an attempt to trace what attention is, why it matters, and how we might begin to reclaim it.

To begin, consider what attention actually is. William James, the philosopher and psychologist, wrote in 1890 that “my experience is what I agree to attend to.” This is a radical statement. It suggests that we are not passive recipients of a pre-existing world but active participants in its creation. The world is infinitely rich, too full of detail for any mind to take in completely. Attention is the filter that selects, from the blooming, buzzing confusion of sensory input, the small slice that becomes our reality. If you spend your morning attending to your breath, the patterns of sunlight on the wall, the taste of coffee, you will have lived a different morning than if you spent it scrolling through news of disasters and strangers’ opinions. Both mornings occur in the same chronological time, but they are not the same life.

The difficulty is that attention feels automatic, but it is shaped by forces we often do not see. In the past two decades, an entire economy has grown up around the harvesting of human attention. Social media platforms, news sites, and apps are built to exploit the brain’s reward systems, offering variable rewards—likes, comments, new posts—that keep us checking and refreshing. The psychologist B.F. Skinner discovered decades ago that intermittent reinforcement is the most powerful way to condition behavior. Slot machines use this principle; so do our phones. Each pull of the scroll may yield something delightful or nothing at all, and that unpredictability keeps the loop running. The result is a population that finds it increasingly difficult to read a book, to sit in silence, to look at a painting for more than a few seconds, or to listen to a friend without glancing at a screen.

This is not a moral failing. It is the predictable outcome of designing technology to maximize engagement rather than human flourishing. The algorithms are not evil; they are simply optimizing for a different goal. But the cost is real. When attention is fragmented, the quality of experience degrades. We skim instead of read. We glance instead of see. We hear instead of listen. The world becomes a blur of impressions, none of them deep enough to leave a lasting mark. The poet Mary Oliver wrote, “Attention is the beginning of devotion.” If she is right, then a distracted life is not merely less productive; it is less devoted, less loving, less alive.

Perhaps the most powerful counterforce to the attention economy is the natural world. Nature does not demand our attention; it simply rewards it. A forest, a shoreline, a mountain, a garden—these places move at a different pace. They are not optimized for engagement. They do not send notifications. They are endlessly complex, but their complexity is patient. When you sit by a river and watch the water, nothing happens, and yet everything happens. The light changes. The current shifts. A fish rises. A leaf falls. The longer you look, the more you see. This is the opposite of the rapid switching required by digital media. It is attention as immersion, as participation, as relationship.

The naturalist and writer Annie Dillard spent a year living by Tinker Creek in Virginia, and her book *Pilgrim at Tinker Creek* is a record of what happens when you pay close, sustained attention to a small patch of earth. She noticed the way a frog’s skin color changes as it is eaten by a giant water bug, the way a cedar tree bends in the wind, the way the same creek looks different every hour of the day. She wrote, “I cannot cause light; the most I can do is try to put myself in the path of its beam.” Attention is like that. We cannot force moments of insight or beauty, but we can place ourselves where they are more likely to occur. We can sit still. We can look closely. We can wait.

There is a tradition in Japanese aesthetics called *mono no aware*, often translated as “the pathos of things” or “an empathy toward things.” It is the awareness of impermanence and the gentle sadness that comes from recognizing the beauty of a passing moment. To practice mono no aware is to attend to the cherry blossoms not despite their brevity but because of it. It is to notice the way the light falls on a bowl of fruit, the sound of rain on a tin roof, the smell of wet earth after a storm. These experiences are available to everyone, but they are missed by those whose attention is elsewhere. The art of noticing is not about adding more experiences to our lives; it is about deepening the ones we already have.

Attention also lies at the heart of love. To love someone is to pay attention to them—not just to their words but to their silences, their gestures, their moods, their needs. The philosopher Iris Murdoch argued that love is “the extremely difficult realization that something other than oneself is real.” This realization requires attention. When we truly listen to another person, we set aside our own mental chatter and make space for their reality. We notice the slight hesitation in their voice, the way they avoid a certain topic, the flicker of joy or pain that crosses their face. This kind of attention is a gift. It says, “You matter. Your experience is worth my time.”

We sit across from loved ones at dinner, half-listening while our minds scroll through to-do lists or our hands rest on the phone in our pocket. We have all been on both sides of this dynamic: speaking to someone who is not fully present, and feeling the subtle hurt of being only half-heard. The remedy is not complicated, but it is difficult. It requires putting the phone away, making eye contact, and choosing to be fully where we are. It requires accepting that we cannot be everywhere at once, and that the person in front of us deserves our whole attention, not the scraps left over after the digital world has taken its share.

Flow occurs when attention is fully focused, when the challenge of the task matches our skills, and when we are free from interruptions. Artists, musicians, writers, scientists, and athletes all describe this state as the source of their best work. But flow is fragile. It takes an average of twenty-three minutes to regain deep focus after an interruption, according to some studies. If we check our email every few minutes, if we respond to every notification, we never enter the sustained concentration that creativity requires. The result is a life of shallow tasks, none of them done with the full force of our abilities.

The poet Rainer Maria Rilke wrote in *Letters to a Young Poet* that “being an artist means not numbering and counting, but ripening like a tree, which does not force its sap and stands confidently in the storms of spring, not afraid that afterward summer may not come.” This ripening requires patience and attention. It requires sitting with an idea long enough for it to develop roots. It requires looking at the world not as a series of problems to be solved but as a mystery to be inhabited. The creative act begins with perception. Before you can write a poem, you must notice something worth writing about. Before you can paint a picture, you must see the light in a way others have not. Before you can compose a song, you must hear the rhythm in everyday life. Attention is the soil in which creativity grows.

Yet modern life has made sustained attention feel almost impossible. We are not only distracted by technology; we are also busy, overcommitted, exhausted. The pace of work has accelerated. The boundaries between work and home have eroded. The expectation of constant availability has become the norm. In such conditions, the idea of sitting still for an hour to read or write or simply think can feel like a luxury, even an indulgence. But attention is not a luxury; it is a necessity. Without it, we lose the ability to reflect, to choose, to act with intention rather than reactivity. We become passive consumers of experience rather than active authors of our own lives.

There is a story about the philosopher Socrates, who was known for stopping in his tracks and standing still for hours, lost in thought. His friends would wait, knowing that he was attending to something in his mind. This kind of stillness is almost unthinkable today. We are uncomfortable with silence, with boredom, with the absence of stimulation. And yet silence is precisely where attention can gather itself. The composer John Cage wrote a piece called *4'33"* in which the performer sits at a piano for four minutes and thirty-three seconds without playing a note. The point is not the absence of music but the presence of the ambient sounds that we normally ignore: the rustle of the audience, the hum of the air conditioner, the distant traffic. Attention to silence reveals that silence is full. The same is true of our inner lives. When we stop filling every moment with noise, we begin to hear the quieter voices of our own thoughts, our own desires, our own questions.

How, then, might we begin to reclaim our attention? The practices are simple to name but difficult to sustain. One is to create periods of intentional solitude. Solitude is not loneliness; it is the choice to be alone with one’s own mind. In solitude, we can read a book without checking our phone. We can take a walk without listening to a podcast. We can sit with a cup of tea and watch the light move across the room. These small acts are not escapes from the world; they are returns to it. By stepping back from the noise, we sharpen our capacity to engage with what matters.

Another practice is to cultivate a habit of close observation. This can be as simple as choosing a small object—a leaf, a stone, a piece of fruit—and looking at it for five minutes, noticing its texture, its color, its shape, its shadows. Or it can be as grand as keeping a journal of daily observations, writing down one thing you noticed each day that you would normally have missed. The point is not to produce great insights but to train the mind to dwell. The artist and educator Frederick Franck wrote a book called *The Zen of Seeing*, in which he describes drawing as a form of meditation. When you draw something, you must look at it with an intensity that most of us rarely exercise. Franck wrote, “I have learned that what I have not drawn, I have never really seen.” Attention is like that. It is the difference between glancing and seeing.

A third practice is to practice listening—to other people, to music, to the natural world. Listening is an act of surrender. You cannot listen while preparing your response. You cannot listen while checking your phone. You must be silent. You must be patient. You must be willing to be changed by what you hear. The Quaker tradition speaks of “listening in silence” as a way of discerning truth. The composer Pauline Oliveros developed a practice called “deep listening,” which she defined as “listening in every possible way to everything possible to hear no matter what you are doing.” This kind of listening is not passive. It is active, engaged, curious. It treats sound as a world to be explored.

Finally, we might practice the art of doing one thing at a time. Multitasking is a myth. The brain does not do two cognitive tasks simultaneously; it switches rapidly between them, and each switch imposes a cost. When we eat, we should eat. When we walk, we should walk. When we talk with a friend, we should talk. This sounds simple, but it is radically countercultural. It means refusing the pressure to optimize every moment, to fill every gap with productivity. It means allowing some experiences to be sufficient in themselves, not as means to an end but as ends in themselves. A meal can be just a meal. A conversation can be just a conversation. A walk can be just a walk. In that just-ness, there is a quiet richness.

At the deepest level, attention is bound up with mortality. We have a finite number of days, a finite number of hours, a finite number of breaths. Every moment we spend in distraction is a moment we will never get back. The Stoic philosopher Seneca wrote that “we are not given a short life but we make it short, and we are not ill-supplied but wasteful of it.” This is not meant to induce anxiety but to inspire clarity. Knowing that time is limited can sharpen our attention. It can help us choose what to notice, what to care about, what to love. The poet William Blake wrote of seeing “a world in a grain of sand and a heaven in a wildflower.” That vision is available to all of us, but it requires attention. It requires the willingness to look at a grain of sand as if it were a world.

I think of the last time I truly paid attention to something beautiful. Perhaps it was the way the morning light caught the edge of a glass of water, creating a small rainbow on the table. Perhaps it was the sound of wind through pine needles, a sound like a distant ocean. Perhaps it was the face of someone I love, seen for a moment not as familiar but as astonishing. These moments are not rare because beauty is rare; they are rare because attention is rare. The world is filled with more beauty than we could ever exhaust. The question is whether we will stop long enough to see it.

The attention economy profits from our distraction, but the choice ultimately remains ours. We can decide to turn off the notifications, to leave the phone in another room, to take a walk without a destination, to look at the sky. We can decide to be present to our own lives. This is not a retreat from the world; it is an engagement with it on a deeper level. It is a small act of resistance, a quiet refusal to live on someone else’s terms. It is the beginning of devotion.

In the end, attention is not about productivity or efficiency. It is about the quality of our presence. It is about whether we are truly here, in this moment, with this person, in this place. It is about whether we see the world as a backdrop for our plans or as a living reality that deserves our regard.
